questions.text: On the Password to Awaiting arrow: what decides that a user goes to Awaiting instead of straight to Signed in, and what exactly is created at that moment?
What is in a pending_logins row, and what does the p2f cookie hold? How does the server connect the cookie to the row when the code is submitted?
What do seal(), enqueue_email() and start_session() each do here, and where is each one called in the flow?
In Setup pending, what is stored in user_totp and in what form (is the secret sealed)? What does the user do to move to 2FA on, and what happens if they abandon setup?
What counts as a failed attempt in Awaiting, what is the limit, and what happens when it is reached or the pending login expires? Is it the Awaiting to Password arrow?
questions.about: Attempts are limited and pending logins expire

questions.text: How does a recovery code get entered during Awaiting, and does using one sign the user in directly? What do the words 'then set up a new authenticator' mean in terms of states?
questions.about: Lost phone: use a recovery code, then set up a new authenticator

questions.text: What does 'Other sessions are handled when 2FA is enabled' mean concretely? Are they ended, kept, or something else?
questions.about: Other sessions are handled when 2FA is enabled

questions.text: What is the Replacement pending state: what starts it, what is stored while it is pending, and does the old authenticator keep working until confirmation?

answers.text: A correct password goes to Awaiting only when the user has an active secret (2FA on, or Replacement pending). The server then inserts a pending_logins row (sha256 of a new random token, user_id, expires_at now plus 5 minutes, wrong_count 0) and sets the p2f cookie to the raw token. No sid cookie is set, so no session exists yet. A user with no active secret goes straight to Signed in through start_session(), as today.

A pending_logins row holds the sha256 of the p2f token, the user_id, expires_at (5 minutes after creation) and wrong_count. The p2f cookie holds the raw random token. On submit, the server hashes the cookie and looks up the row, the same way it looks up sessions. The row is deleted on success, expiry or the fifth wrong entry.

Checked in existing/login.py and existing/schema.sql. seal() encrypts the TOTP secret into user_totp (setup, step 1), and unseal() reads it for the code check. start_session() creates the session and sid cookie in step 7 (no 2FA), step 10 (valid app code) and step 11 (recovery code). enqueue_email() is called only in step 11, when a recovery code is used, and it does not block the sign-in.

In Setup pending, user_totp holds the new secret in pending_secret, sealed with seal(), and secret stays empty. The user moves to 2FA on by typing a valid code (step 3), which moves the sealed secret into secret and issues 10 hashed recovery codes. If the user abandons setup, the state stays Setup pending, 2FA stays off and sign-in is unaffected. The next setup start overwrites the pending secret. The brief sets no expiry for setup, so none is added.

A wrong entry in Awaiting is a wrong app code, or a recovery code that is unknown or already used. The limit is 5 wrong entries (wrong_count) or 5 minutes from the password check, whichever comes first. Either one deletes the pending row, clears p2f and returns the user to the Password step. Yes, that is the Awaiting to Password arrow. A wrong password is not counted here, because it happens before the pending login exists.

The code page accepts an app code or a recovery code. A recovery code is matched against the user's unused hashes. A match signs the user in directly (Awaiting to Signed in), deletes that code and queues the email. The words 'set up a new authenticator' mean that the signed-in user starts a replacement from Security settings (On to Replacement pending). That needs no code from the old app, because the recovery code has just proved the user's identity.

Other sessions means every row in sessions for that user except the current one. They are deleted, so those cookies stop working at once. The plan applies this when 2FA is first confirmed (Setup pending to 2FA on). The brief does not say whether a replacement also does it, so that case is left open in the file's open questions.

Replacement pending is started by a signed-in user who already has 2FA on. The new sealed secret is stored in pending_secret, and secret still holds the active one. Sign-in keeps using secret until the new app's code is confirmed, which the brief requires. If the user never confirms, the old authenticator keeps working and the pending secret remains until the user starts again or turns 2FA off.

questions.text: In step 3 the server deletes every other session of the user. What identifies 'the current session', and is the session the user signed in with at setup the only one that survives?
At sign-in with a recovery code (step 11), is last_used_step touched, and does the recovery code count as a 'valid code' for replay protection in any way?
What exactly does 'replay' protect against in step 10? If the user types the same valid code twice within 30 seconds, what does the second attempt do, and is last_used_step updated on success?
If a user with 2FA on signs in twice quickly, creating two pending_logins rows, what happens to the first row and cookie? Can one user have several pending rows at once?
questions.about: pending_logins (one row per sign-in in progress)

questions.text: In step 13, the user is signed in and enters the password and a code. Does turning 2FA off also end other sessions, and does it clear any pending_logins rows for that user?

In the state diagram, ReplacePending goes to Off with password plus code. Which secret is the code checked against there: the active secret, the pending secret, or either? And in step 13 for Setup pending (secret empty), is there anything to turn off?
questions.about: The state diagram: ReplacePending --> Off, step 13

questions.text: In step 5 when the new secret becomes active, what happens to last_used_step, and what does the email in step 11 'how many remain' count come from?

answers.text: The current session is the one whose sid cookie, hashed with sha256, matches a row in sessions.token_hash. Logout looks it up the same way in existing/login.py. Step 3 deletes every other session row of that user, so the matched row is the only one that survives. Setup can only start while signed in, so the current session always exists at that point. The file now says this in step 3.

No. A recovery code does not change last_used_step and is not checked for replay. last_used_step guards TOTP codes only. A recovery code is deleted on use, so it cannot be reused. The reason is that the brief asks for replay protection on time steps, and a recovery code has no time step. Step 11 now says this.

Replay protection stops the same app code from being accepted twice in its window, for example a code seen over someone's shoulder or a double submit. The second attempt is rejected, because its step is not later than last_used_step, and it counts as a wrong entry. On success, step 10 sets last_used_step to the accepted step. The first draft did not say this, so step 10 now does. The brief requires that a used step be rejected.

Each correct password deletes any earlier pending row for that user before it creates one (step 8). The older browser's p2f cookie then points to no row, and step 9 sends that browser to the password page. One row per user keeps the wrong-entry count simple. The reason is the same restart rule as the brief. The open question on attempt limits records that a user with the password can restart the count, bounded only by the login rate limit.

Turning 2FA off does not end other sessions. The brief asks for that only when 2FA is first confirmed, and says nothing about turning it off, so the plan does not add it. Turning off does delete that user's pending_logins rows (step 13), so a login begun while 2FA was on cannot finish after 2FA is off. The session question is listed in the open questions.

Only the active secret (user_totp.secret) is checked. A pending secret has never been confirmed, so it has not proved the user has the app, and it cannot authorise turning 2FA off. In Setup pending, 2FA is already off, so there is no turn-off action. The pending secret stays until the next setup, as step 1 says. Step 13 now says both things.

last_used_step belongs to the user, not to one secret. It is not reset when a replacement starts, because resetting it would drop replay protection for the old app while it still works. The confirming code from the new app must be later than the last accepted step, and then it sets last_used_step. The cost is that a new-app code in the same 30-second window as the last old-app sign-in is rejected until the next step. Step 5 and the notes say so. On the email count: it is the number of the user's recovery_codes rows left after the used one is deleted, so it starts at 9 after the first use. This is checked against step 11 in the plan, not against code.

questions.text: In step 9 the code page 'accepts an app code or a recovery code'. How does the server tell which one the user typed, and is it one input field or two?
questions.about: Step 9: the code page is opened or posted

questions.text: In step 10, how does the server check an app code: does it unseal() the active secret and compute the codes for three time steps? What happens when two of those steps are valid but one is already used?
In step 3, is the whole confirm one transaction that also deletes the other sessions? What does the user see if the code is right but the transaction fails?

On step 12, when wrong_count reaches 5 and the user is sent to the password page, can they sign in again at once with the same password and get a fresh 5 tries? Is anything else recorded about the failures?
In step 13, which exact password and code checks happen and in what order, and what does 'signed in' mean if the session is the one used to turn 2FA off? Does the current session stay?
In step 9, who deletes an expired pending_logins row if nobody opens the code page again? Does the expired row block a new sign-in in step 8?
questions.about: Notes on the diagram: Nothing runs in the background

answers.text: One input field. A 6-digit value is checked as an app code, and any other value as a recovery code. Recovery codes are never six digits, so the server can tell them apart by shape. One field keeps the page simple. Step 9 now says this.

Yes. The server unseals the active secret and computes the code for the current step and the steps either side. It accepts the matching step only if that step is later than last_used_step. A typed code matches one step, because each step gives a different code. If that step is already used, the code is rejected. Step 10 now says this and names the active secret, not the pending one.

Yes. Step 3 is one database transaction, and it also deletes the other sessions. If the code is right but the transaction fails, nothing changes. The pending secret stays, last_used_step is not set and no codes are shown. The user sees an error and can submit a code again. Step 3 now says this.

Yes. The fifth wrong entry deletes the pending row, so the next correct password starts a new pending login with 5 fresh tries. Nothing else is recorded: there is no failure log and no account lock. The only bound is the login rate limit of 10 per minute per IP, which the open question on attempt limits already records. No change to the file.

The request must carry a valid sid cookie, as any Security settings page does. The server checks the password first, then the code, and deletes nothing unless both pass. The current session stays signed in, because it is the session that made the request. Other sessions are not ended. Step 13 now says this.

Nobody deletes it until someone next touches it. Step 9 deletes it when the code page is opened, and step 8 deletes it when the same user signs in again. Until then it stays in the table but is ignored, because it has expired. It does not block step 8, because step 8 deletes any existing row for the user, expired or not. Bulk cleanup stays in the open questions. Step 8 now says this.

teachbacks.text:
I'll follow one user from turning on 2FA to signing in with it, then cover the other paths.

1. **Setup starts.** A signed-in user clicks Set up in Security settings. The server makes a random secret, seals it with `seal()` and writes it to `user_totp.pending_secret`. It shows a QR code for the authenticator app. The account is now "Setup pending". Sign-in ignores the pending secret. If the user clicks Set up again, the old pending secret is overwritten. If the user leaves, 2FA stays off and the pending secret stays until the next setup.

2. **Confirm the code.** The user types the 6-digit code from the app. The server runs the "code check" against `pending_secret`. It computes the code for each of 3 time steps (the current 30-second step, the one before and the one after) and accepts a match only if that step is later than `last_used_step`. The check writes nothing, and the caller saves the step. A wrong code changes nothing and the user can retry.

3. **Turn on.** On a valid code, one database transaction does four things. It moves `pending_secret` into `secret`. It sets `last_used_step` to the accepted step. It deletes all old recovery codes and inserts 10 new ones as sha256 hashes. It deletes every other session of the user. The kept session is the one whose `sid` cookie hashes to a `sessions.token_hash`. The 10 raw codes are shown once in this response. The account is now "2FA on". If the transaction fails, it rolls back, the user sees an error and no codes are shown. The pending secret is kept, so the user can enter a code again.

4. **Later sign-in: password.** The user posts email and password. The password check is unchanged. A wrong password returns the same 401 as today and creates nothing.

5. **Branch on the active secret.** If there is no active secret (2FA off, or Setup pending), the server calls `start_session()` straight away. That creates the `sessions` row and sets the `sid` cookie. If there is an active secret (2FA on, or Replacement pending), the flow continues at step 6.

6. **Pending login created.** The server deletes any existing `pending_logins` row for this user, expired or not. It inserts a new row with the `token_hash` of a new random token, the `user_id`, `expires_at` (now plus 5 minutes) and `wrong_count` 0. It sets the `p2f` cookie to the raw token (httponly, secure, samesite Lax, 5-minute max age) and redirects to the code page. No `sid` is set, so there is no session yet. An older browser with an old `p2f` cookie now has no matching row.

7. **Code page.** Each time the page is opened or posted, the server hashes the `p2f` cookie and looks up the row. If there is no row, it clears `p2f` and redirects to the password page. If the row has expired, it deletes the row, clears `p2f` and redirects to the password page. Expiry is only noticed here, because nothing runs in the background. Otherwise it shows one input. A 6-digit value goes to step 8. Anything else goes to step 9.

8. **App code.** The server runs the code check against the active `secret`, never the pending one. On a match it sets `last_used_step` to that step, deletes the pending row, clears `p2f` and calls `start_session()`. The user is signed in.

9. **Recovery code.** The server hashes the value and looks for an unused hash for this user. On a match it deletes that code and the pending row, clears `p2f`, calls `start_session()` and calls `enqueue_email()`. The email says a recovery code was used and how many remain, which is 9 after the first use. The email goes through a background queue that retries, so a send failure does not affect the sign-in. `last_used_step` is not changed.

10. **Wrong entry.** A wrong app code (outside the drift window, or a step already used), or an unknown or used recovery code, adds 1 to `wrong_count`. At 5, the server deletes the pending row, clears `p2f` and sends the user to the password page. Below 5, the user stays on the code page.

11. **Replacing the authenticator.** A signed-in user with 2FA on starts a replacement. The server seals a new secret into `pending_secret` and leaves `secret` alone, so the old app keeps working. Starting again overwrites the pending secret. When the user enters a valid code from the new app, the server checks it against `pending_secret`. One transaction then moves `pending_secret` into `secret`, sets `last_used_step`, and replaces the 10 recovery codes with 10 new ones, shown once. Other sessions are not ended. If the transaction fails, it rolls back, the old app still works and no codes are shown. Because `last_used_step` is kept, a code from the new app in the same 30-second step as the last old-app sign-in is rejected until the next step.

12. **Turning 2FA off.** The user is signed in (valid `sid`) with 2FA on or Replacement pending. They enter the password and a valid app code or unused recovery code in Security settings. The server checks the password first, then the code, against `secret` and never `pending_secret`. Only if both pass does it delete the `user_totp` row, all the user's `recovery_codes`, and the user's `pending_logins`. The current session stays signed in and other sessions are not ended. If either check fails, nothing is deleted.

13. **Lost phone.** The user signs in with an unused recovery code (step 9), starts a replacement and confirms it with the new app. No old-app code is needed. This gives 10 new recovery codes.
gaps: The document does not say what the user sees or what status or message the server returns for a wrong code on the setup confirm (step 2) or on the code page (step 10). It only says the user may retry or stays on the code page.
It does not say what gets the setup code (step 2) or turn-off code (step 12) retry limit. The document says no limit is decided there.

It does not say what the Set up or start-replacement request carries to prove the user is signed in beyond 'while signed in'. For turn-off it names the `sid` cookie, but for setup and replacement the check is not spelled out.
It does not say what `seal()` and `unseal()` do on KMS failure, or whether a KMS failure during sign-in code checks makes the request fail.

It does not say whether a recovery-code wrong entry still counts toward `wrong_count` when the pending row has just been created in a new login that replaced an older one. Specifically, the document does not say what happens to a browser holding the older pending login's `p2f` beyond sending it to the password page.
It does not say how the 5-minute `expires_at` is compared with 'now' at the code page, for example which clock or time source the server uses.

It does not say how the `last_used_step` update and the code check are protected against two simultaneous requests using the same code (the check writes nothing and the caller saves the step, but no locking is described).
